title: Progressive delay does not bound password guessing under concurrent requests and the stated maximum guess rate is unproven
evidence: Resolved against the verification criterion at the PRD level. The US-13 preamble (L269) sets one slot per email covering an attempt that is 'waiting or being checked'. Other attempts get the generic failure 'without checking the password', and 'the slot is free again only when the holder's check has ended'. My own check of the bound: in any 900-second window, check k (k >= 2) saw f >= k-1 on arrival, so its delay is at least delay(k-1). That gives 15 + 16(n-7) <= 900, so n <= 62, which matches NFR-15 (L322) and OQ-46 (L471). AC-13.13 (L283) is the staggered scenario the verification asked for: every 3 s for 5 minutes, 15 IPs at about 7 each (within per-IP limits), at most 24 checks, identical responses for existing and unknown emails. It tells the designs apart: about 21 checks under the correct mechanism, about 90 under the old 5-per-email cap or a slot that covers only the check. AC-13.11 (L281) now expects exactly 1 check, which matches the mechanism. The per-email 429 is removed from AC-13.12 (L282). The integration-test part of the verification (burst and staggered) is a Phase 6/7 item and cannot be checked yet.
rationale: Reported as resolved for the orchestrator to set the status. Severity is unchanged for the record. The remaining part (integration tests for AC-13.11 and AC-13.13) is traced to Phase 6/7.
recommended_fix: None at PRD level. QA must build AC-13.11 and AC-13.13 as integration tests that fail against a slot that covers only the check.
verification: Integration tests for AC-13.11 and AC-13.13 pass, and a mutation (the slot released when the delay ends) makes AC-13.13 fail.

fingerprint: sha1(operations/alerting|docs/requirements/customer-checkout-with-order-history.md|alert conditions have no deduplication and the sign-in cap alert can be triggered by any client)
title: Alert conditions have no deduplication and the sign-in cap alert can be triggered by any client
evidence: Partially resolved. The sign-in cap part is resolved. NFR-22 (L329) and AC-7.6 (L203) aggregate the service-wide cap to 'one alert per 15 minutes with a count', the per-IP cap is audited only, and AC-7.6 contains the '100 cap events in 5 minutes ... at most one cap alert, while a mismatch in the same window still alerts' test. The verification also asked for deduplication 'per condition', and that is still missing: (a) 'more than 10 rejected callbacks in 5 minutes' is labelled low severity but has no grouping rule. Anyone can trigger it from any IP (invalid-signature callbacks are allowed at 60 per minute per IP, L346), so a continuous stream could produce an alert every 5 minutes indefinitely. (b) Long-running conditions ('job missing 2 consecutive runs', 'provider error rate above 20% over 5 minutes') are 'once per event', but the PRD does not say what one event is for a condition that lasts an hour (one alert, or one per evaluation window).
rationale: An attacker who can trigger repeated low-severity alerts still adds noise for the single operator. An outage with no defined grouping produces either one alert or dozens. This is an operational-toil risk.
recommended_fix: In NFR-22, state that the rejected-callback alert is grouped like the cap alert (one per 15 minutes with a count), and that long-running payment conditions alert once when they start, re-alert at a stated interval (for example 60 minutes) while active, and send a recovery notice.
verification: NFR-22 gives a grouping rule for every listed condition. AC-7.6 includes '30 minutes of continuous invalid callbacks produce at most 2 rejected-callback alerts' and 'a 60-minute provider outage produces 1 start alert, at most 1 reminder and 1 recovery notice'.

fingerprint: sha1(security/open-redirect|docs/requirements/customer-checkout-with-order-history.md|return target rule does not require redirecting to the validated normalised value)
title: Return target rule does not require redirecting to the validated normalised value
evidence: Partially resolved. AC-13.7 (L277) now states 'The redirect uses the path, query and fragment of the parsed, validated URL, never the raw input, and no further decoding happens after validation', and includes `/%252F%252Fevil.example` among the negative examples that 'land on the catalogue'. But the stated rule does not produce that result. The raw value starts with '/%' (a single '/' not followed by '/' or '\'), so it passes the raw check. Decoding once gives `/%2F%2Fevil.example`, which parses against our origin as a same-origin path, so it passes the origin check. It contains no control characters. The rule therefore accepts it and redirects to the same-origin path `/%2F%2Fevil.example`. That is safe (no open redirect), but it is not 'the catalogue'. An implementation that follows the rule exactly fails this negative example, and the developer would either add an unstated rule or loosen the test.
rationale: An expected result that the stated rule cannot produce invites a silent interpretation or a weakened assertion later (guide 9.3).
recommended_fix: Either add a rule, 'the once-decoded value must not contain "%" (no multiply-encoded input)', so that the example lands on the catalogue, or change the expected result for `/%252F%252Fevil.example` to 'stays on our origin (never reaches evil.example)'.
verification: Each negative example in AC-13.7 produces its stated result when only the stated rule is applied.

fingerprint: sha1(data-integrity/payments|docs/requirements/customer-checkout-with-order-history.md|early close of a pending order with an open provider session does not require cancelling the session and duplicate review covers only expired orders)
title: Early close of a pending order with an open provider session does not require cancelling the session and duplicate review covers only expired orders
evidence: AC-3.18 (L153, new in revision 8) closes an order whose provider session is still open (minutes 20 to 25) when 'Pay' is chosen with less than 5 minutes left: 'the old order is cancelled after the provider confirms no payment was taken'. AC-3.15 (L150) and AC-3.17 (L152) use the same wording, and REQ-23 (L103) says only 'closed early after provider confirmation'. None of them requires the server to cancel the old provider session first. AC-3.9 (L144: 'after the provider confirms its session is closed') and AC-4.3 (L161: 'the server cancels the provider session and confirms') do. A lookup showing 'no payment yet' leaves the old hosted page payable until minute 25. A customer who reaches 'Pay' at minute 24 has, by definition, opened that hosted page before, possibly in another tab, and can still complete it while the new order's session is also live. The result is two charges for the same cart. The old order then becomes paid through the late-success path (AC-4.7, L165, which does alert). But AC-4.11 (L169), the only rule that flags `duplicate_payment_review`, applies only when 'order A ... expired', not when it was cancelled by an early close.
rationale: This is a double-charge path created by the new 5-minute minimum-lifetime rule, in a Tier 3 money flow. Impact is limited because the provider is in test mode, the window is at most 5 minutes, and the late-success alert still fires. That makes it Medium rather than High.
recommended_fix: In REQ-23 and AC-3.15/3.17/3.18, state that the server cancels the old provider session at the provider and confirms it is closed with no payment taken before creating the new order (as AC-3.9 and AC-4.3 do). Widen AC-4.11 to 'order A expired, cancelled or failed' so any second paid order for the same cart version is flagged `duplicate_payment_review`.
verification: AC-3.18 includes: 'Given the old hosted page is still open in another tab, when I complete payment on it after choosing Pay at minute 24, then the provider rejects it (session cancelled), and at most 1 successful charge results'. AC-4.11 covers a cancelled order A.

fingerprint: sha1(security/authentication|docs/requirements/customer-checkout-with-order-history.md|per-email sign-in slot has no release rule for crashed instances or abandoned requests)
title: Per-email sign-in slot has no release rule for crashed instances or abandoned requests
evidence: The US-13 preamble (L269) says 'The slot is free again only when the holder's check has ended'. The slot lives in a shared store (A-9 L361, D-8 L374). Nothing says what happens if the API instance holding the slot crashes or restarts during the up-to-16-second delay. Nothing says whether a client disconnect cancels the hold, and if so whether the slot is freed. If the slot is never released, that email can never get a password check again: a hard lockout, which REQ-19 forbids ('no hard lockout').
rationale: This is a design matter for Phase 4 (the lease on the shared store), so it is a Low note for the architect. It should still be bounded in the requirement, because without a bound one incident becomes a permanent lockout.
recommended_fix: Add to the preamble or A-9: 'the slot is a lease that expires no later than the maximum delay plus the hash time plus a margin (for example 20 s), and a client disconnect still runs or abandons the check and frees the slot'. The architect chooses how in Phase 4.
verification: An AC or ADR test: kill the instance holding the slot, and the next attempt for that email after the lease ends gets a password check.

fingerprint: sha1(security/session|docs/requirements/customer-checkout-with-order-history.md|automatic payment status checks may extend the 30-minute idle session timeout)
title: Automatic payment status checks may extend the 30-minute idle session timeout
evidence: AC-4.4 (L162, new text) has the page check status automatically every 5 seconds 'until the order is expired'. NFR-14 (L321) and AC-13.4 (L274) set a 30-minute idle timeout. Nothing says whether the automatic checks count as user activity. If they do, an unattended tab keeps the session alive with no user present for up to the 30-minute order lifetime, and longer if more than one pending order is cycled. The PRD also does not say whether checking stops at a final state, or what the page does when a check returns 401 (AC-4.9 covers only the return from the provider).
rationale: Background polling that resets idle timers is a known session-management weakness (OWASP ASVS V3). The impact is limited, because polling is bounded by order expiry and the data is synthetic.
recommended_fix: State in AC-4.4 that automatic checks do not reset the idle timer, that checking stops at a final state or on HTTP 401 (followed by the AC-13.4 sign-in redirect), or explicitly accept the extension.
verification: AC-4.4 states whether polling counts as activity and when it stops. A test with a tab left idle on 'payment processing' for 30 minutes shows the session expires as NFR-14 requires.

fingerprint: sha1(operations/jobs|docs/requirements/customer-checkout-with-order-history.md|reconciliation pass bound of 60 seconds is unachievable sequentially during a provider outage and may trigger job-missed alerts)
title: Reconciliation pass bound of 60 seconds is unachievable sequentially during a provider outage and may trigger job-missed alerts
evidence: REQ-24 (L104) bounds a pass at 60 s including 10 s provider timeouts. During an outage (AC-4.12, L170), every lookup takes the full 10 s, so more than 6 pending orders processed one after another overrun the pass. It is not defined whether an overrunning pass counts as a 'missed run' under NFR-22 (L329), which would raise high-severity job alerts on top of the provider-error alert.
rationale: Design detail for Phase 4 (parallel lookups, a circuit breaker, a definition of a missed run). It is noted for the architect and does not block the PRD.
recommended_fix: In the Phase 4 ADR for D-7, set lookup parallelism or a circuit breaker so the 60-second bound holds during outages, and define 'missed run'.
verification: The ADR states the parallelism or circuit breaker and the missed-run definition. A test with 50 pending orders and a provider stub that times out keeps the pass within 60 s and raises no job-missed alert.
